One of the most useful things I do after a market cycle is study the biggest winners I didn’t catch.

I find the stocks that ran the most during that period and work backward: where was my setup, what was the market doing, and why didn’t I participate? https://t.co/rqmFbjTUje

I look for an entry that actually fits my rules: a pullback into the rising 21ema-structure, without excessive weekly extension.

Picking the lowest candle afterward teaches me little. If the stock never offered my setup, I accept that. Not every winner has to be mine.

My journal shows the trades I took. It doesn’t show the opportunities I overlooked or hesitated on.

First question: Was the stock in my universe? Was it showing strong stock and group RS? Missing a leader in preparation is different from seeing my setup and failing to act.

Then I put the market chart beside it. Was breadth improving? Were leaders holding up while the indexes still looked messy?

Did the entry require taking a small position early in the turn, before conditions felt comfortable? What evidence supported that decision at the time?

Free in https://t.co/GEJpgVvdaY (including full-year historical data ;))

I also review the failed setups from that same period. Studying only the eventual winners makes early participation look much easier than it was.

I need to account for the uncertainty and small losses I might have faced while trying to establish exposure around the turn.

If a valid entry was there, why did I pass? Had recent losses made me demand more confirmation? Was I waiting for a deeper pullback that never came?

Reviewing the whole cycle helps me see how the previous difficult stretch influenced my decisions when opportunities improved.

Try this after your next market cycle: choose three big winners you missed and put each beside the market chart.

Find the first entry that fits your rules. Write down what you knew then and why you passed. You may find something to improve—or a move that simply wasn’t yours.

https://t.co/v0rLpDgeCR

The review should lead to a specific improvement: a better universe, earlier preparation, or clearer conditions for taking a small test.

If I caught the stock but sold quickly, I examine my exit. Was it justified, or did discomfort keep me from holding a valid position?

One of the biggest differences in trading comes when you stop trying to make money from a loser.

You will never get ahead spending time and money on a losing stock.

And unlike most people here - I have had my fair share of losers.

I have averaged down on positions.
I have spent months just trying to break even.
A position I wanted to hold for a week went on for 6 months.
I have locked up my capital in a losing stock while every good idea walked right past me.

You will make that money back - and more - just by trading normally.

If you're in a losing position, the best thing you can do is this:

Accept you were wrong. Cut your losses. Move on.

The fears around $BMNR potentially moving from ~5% toward 10% of ETH supply seem overly focused on dilution.

I think $MSTR provides an important lesson here.

When a DAT trades above NAV, that premium becomes a source of capital. Shares can be issued above the value of the crypto backing them and the proceeds recycled into more crypto. Done correctly, share count rises while ETH per share and NAV per share can rise with it.

This is incredibly important for a DAT. If you can’t monetize an mNAV materially above 1x to create per-share value, there is little fundamental reason for that premium to persist.

That’s the flywheel:

Above NAV → accretive issuance → more ETH per share.
Below NAV → accretive buybacks → more ETH per share.

And this is where I think the criticism of BMNR’s 10% ambition gets somewhat backwards.

10% isn’t what justifies dilution. 
Accretive economics justify dilution.

But the ambition to keep accumulating ETH, whether the eventual number is 7%, 10% or something else, gives BMNR somewhere productive to deploy the capital created by its equity premium.

In other words, the thing people are worried about can, if BMNR adheres to strict mNAV discipline, be exactly what shareholders should want:

A mandate to keep converting an expensive equity currency into greater ETH and NAV per share.

MSTR showed how powerful that flywheel can become at scale if done right before the recent blunders. BMNR adds staking economics on top.

What @fundstrat needs to make crystal clear is the rule: don’t dilute to hit 10%. Dilute when it is accretive. Buy back when the discount makes that accretive.

The goal isn’t 10% at any cost.

The goal is maximizing ETH and NAV per share, and using the ambition to accumulate more ETH as the engine that keeps the flywheel running.

(See below shares outstanding and MNAV on $MSTR, you need it all to have a chance at 2+ MNAV in a final cycle move)

If I was on the $BMNR board, I think the next step would be to make the long-term capital allocation framework extremely clear to shareholders.

The objective shouldn’t be 10% of ETH supply at any cost, nor should it be stopping at 5% and simply becoming a passive ETH wrapper.

The objective should be long-term accretion in ETH per share and NAV per share.

That means treating the cycle opportunistically. 

When mNAV provides attractive economics, use the equity premium to grow the treasury accretively. When the stock trades at a meaningful discount, be willing to repurchase shares. When neither opportunity exists, wait.

There doesn’t need to be a deadline for reaching 10%. Crypto cycles are long, and the ability to be patient is part of the advantage.

I think @fundstrat / Tom Lee could remove a lot of the current uncertainty simply by communicating this framework clearly and then reporting against it every quarter:

ETH/share. 
NAV/share. 
mNAV. 
Staking income. 
Average mNAV of issuance. 
Average mNAV of repurchases. 
—
Resulting per-share accretion.

Give investors the framework and the numbers to judge execution.

10% can remain the ambition. Per-share accretion should be the mandate.

I think that would go a long way toward aligning management and shareholders around what the next phase of $BMNR is actually trying to accomplish.

There needs to be an understanding of the investor base.

The people who really got hurt were those buying at 2–3x mNAV and paying an enormous premium for the underlying ETH.

Since then, the increase in share count has also come with substantial growth in ETH per share. That’s the distinction I’m making.

More shares outstanding ≠ automatically being diluted economically.

If BMNR issues above NAV and turns that premium into more ETH/NAV per share, existing shareholders are being accreted to, not diluted in underlying value.

The price you pay for that NAV is a separate question.

Dilution is not a bad thing if you get value for it on the balance sheet. 

It ends up being all about at what MNAV you bought in at as long as you dilute above 1MNAV to buy ETH and do buybacks under 1.

BMNR has been very good in my view about not diluting under 1 MNAV much.
